content: Goldman Sachs (GS) is trading at $929.61, above its 7-, 20-, 50-, 12-, and 26-day moving averages, but still below immediate resistance at $937.45 and strong resistance at $945.30. Binance Futures ... Goldman Sachs (GS) is up 0.93% on the session to $929.61, with the market trading between $913.92 and $933.53 over the last 24 hours. That puts GS above its short- and medium-term moving averages — SMA 7 at $897.93, SMA 20 at $899.75, SMA 50 at $900.26, EMA 12 at $903.68, and EMA 26 at $901.58 — which is consistent with an oversold rebound attempt. GS is also trading near the upper Bollinger Band at $942.66, with a %B position of 0.8479, which places price close to resistance rather than deep in trend expansion. The MACD histogram is flat at 0.0000, so there is no clear momentum edge from that indicator. The pivot point sits at $925.69, and price is holding just above it for now. Immediate support is marked at $917.84, followed by stronger support at $906.08. On the upside, immediate resistance is $937.45, with stronger resistance at $945.30. The current setup leans on price holding above the pivot and defending $917.84. A break back below that area would weaken the oversold-rebound case and put $906.08 back in play. title: John Summit Drops Official Remix of Karol G’s ‘BbY WOW’ - EDMTunes
content:
John Summit has officially released his remix of Karol G‘s ‘BbY WOW,’ out now via Experts Only/Bichota Records. The Chicago-born, Miami-based producer first tested the edit live during a September show in Bogotá, Colombia, reworking one of the year’s biggest Latin pop crossover hits into something built for his own tech house sets. Since that first run-out, the remix has stuck around as a fixture of Summit’s live shows, generating the kind of crowd reaction that usually pushes an unofficial edit toward a proper release. That’s exactly what happened here, with Karol G’s camp and Bichota Records signing off on an official version rather than leaving it to bootleg YouTube rips and festival set recordings. The timing lines up with another notable crossover moment between the two artists. Last week, Summit made a surprise appearance at Karol G’s release celebration for No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto in Mexico City, joining her onstage to perform the remix together for the first time. The pairing of Summit’s club-oriented production with the original’s Latin pop and reggaetón DNA underscored just how far his sound has traveled beyond the house and techno circuit he built his name in. The celebration included a full live performance of Karol G’s 14-track album and streamed globally on TikTok LIVE, reportedly becoming one of the platform’s most-watched livestreams to date. The remix arrives in the middle of the most expansive tour run of Summit’s career. He’s currently crisscrossing North American arenas in support of his album CTRL ESCAPE, released back in April, a project that fuses tech house with dubstep, drum & bass, and other influences Summit has been slowly folding into his sets over the past couple years. Dates on the current leg include stops at Chicago’s United Center, Miami’s Kaseya Center, and a sold-out show at Brooklyn’s Barclays Center on November 28. Once the North American run wraps, Summit heads overseas for European dates before closing out the year with festival stops in Australia and New Zealand. The tour follows a run of milestones that have defined Summit’s 2026, including a hometown headline set at Lollapalooza, his debut Ibiza residency at [UNVRS], and the return of his Experts Only Festival to New York, which pulled in 60,000 fans across two days at Randall’s Island. Summit’s label, Experts Only, has become the banner under which he’s staged everything from Tennessee hill takeovers to snow-covered events in Vail and Tahoe. A former CPA, Summit has built a catalog that includes over three billion global streams, two number one U.S. dance radio hits, and eleven Top 10 entries on the Billboard Hot Electronic/Dance Songs chart. His 2024 debut album Comfort In Chaos explored themes of vice and virtue, while CTRL ESCAPE reframes that same tension around the push and pull between the 9-to-5 grind and the release of the rave. title: Study finds European motorcycle industry generates £30 billion in GDP - Visordown
content: An Oxford Economics study has found that the European motorcycle industry generates around £30 billion in GDP. A newly published study has found that the European motorcycle industry generates almost £30 billion in GDP. Motorcycling in Europe feels constantly under pressure to justify itself. In the UK, October saw year-to-year growth for the motorcycle industry of over 10 per cent in terms of registrations, yet MCIA CEO Tony Campbell said after the figures were published that the UK government still does not realise the true value and significance of the country’s motorcycle sector.’ In Europe, Antonio Perlot, the secretary general of the manufacturers’ association, ACEM, has conducted a study with Oxford Economics into the impact of the motorcycle industry on the European economy. The findings of the study are stark: 481,600 jobs and €35 billion (£29 billion) in GDP, a popular measure of a country’s economic strength. €26 billion of that overall GDP contribution comes from making, selling, and repairing motorcycles, while €5 billion comes from equipment like helmets and other riding gear, and €2.7 billion comes from racing and other events. The study also found that the trade gap – the difference between imports and exports – for European motorcycling had doubled since 2019, from a €1 billion gap to €2 billion, in favour of imports. It’s therefore not only a study that shows the importance of the European motorcycle industry to the region itself, but also highlights the risks it faces at present and therefore the importance of political support for it. The study was presented by ACEM at EICMA, where Perlot said it gives a “complete picture” of the value of motorcycling to Europe. “This study gives us a complete picture of what motorcycling brings to Europe: €35 billion in value, almost half a million jobs and real benefits for the way people move in cities,” said Antonio Perlot, ACEM Secretary General. “But these figures cannot be taken for granted. To stay competitive, European manufacturers need fair and reciprocal access to global markets, motorcycles fully integrated in urban mobility planning and, above all, conditions supporting manufacturers’ continued investment in Europe.” Mariano Roman, President of Confindustria ANCMA, added: “These figures confirm the value of an industry that creates jobs, skills and innovation, and in which Italy is one of Europe’s leading players. “EICMA is its global point of reference: the place where the motorcycle industry presents its future and engages with markets, the public and institutions. Bringing this debate here means linking the sector’s economic and social value to the choices needed to sustain it. “Growth in registrations does not automatically translate into higher production and profitability: to keep investing and innovating in Europe, we need clear and proportionate rules, reciprocity in trade and full recognition of two-wheelers in mobility policies.” Stay up to speed with the latest motorcycling news and analysis, delivered straight to your inbox. title: Tripura Inducts 3 Senior TPS Officers into IPS, DGP G.S. Rao Confers Insignia at Ceremony - Indian Masterminds
content: Home » News » Bureaucracy News » Tripura Inducts 3 Senior TPS Officers into IPS, DGP G.S. Rao Confers Insignia at Ceremony AGARTALA: Tripura Police has received a boost to its senior leadership with the induction of three Tripura Police Service (TPS) officers into the Indian Police Service (IPS). The newly promoted officers are Kishore Debbarma, Rajib Nag and Rajib Sengupta, who have been allocated to the Tripura cadre following their elevation under the prescribed promotion framework. To mark the occasion, a ceremonial piping event was organised at the Police Headquarters on Thursday. During the ceremony, Tripura Director General of Police (DGP) G.S. Rao, a 1999-batch Indian Police Service (IPS) officer of the Tripura cadre, formally adorned the three officers with the IPS insignia. The event was attended by senior police officials and colleagues, who congratulated the officers on their elevation to one of the country’s premier All India Services. The induction marks an important milestone in their careers and recognises their years of service in the Tripura Police. The induction follows a notification issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on November 6, 2026, appointing Kishore Debbarma, Rajib Nag and Rajib Sengupta to the Indian Police Service under the Select List of 2025. The appointments have been made in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Police Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, and the Indian Police Service (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations, 1955. Under the promotion process, eligible officers of the State Police Service are considered for induction into the IPS through the prescribed selection and appointment framework. With this notification, all three officers have formally entered the IPS and have been allocated to the Tripura cadre. Read also: Tripura DGP Charge: Why 1999-Batch GS Rao Was Given Additional Responsibility Despite Senior IPS Officers As part of their induction into the Indian Police Service, all three officers will undergo a one-year probation period along with mandatory induction training, as prescribed under the applicable IPS regulations. The training programme is intended to familiarise promoted officers with the administrative, operational and leadership responsibilities associated with the IPS. It will also prepare them to handle higher-level responsibilities within the police administration and strengthen their understanding of the broader functioning of the All India Service. The Ministry of Home Affairs notification has clarified that the appointments will remain subject to the final outcome of the pending Special Leave Petition (Civil) Nos. 19765–19767 of 2015. The matter relates to the case of State of Tripura and Others versus Jayanta Chakraborty and Others. Accordingly, the induction of the three officers is subject to the final decision in the pending legal proceedings. The elevation of Kishore Debbarma, Rajib Nag and Rajib Sengupta is being viewed as recognition of their service and contributions to law enforcement in Tripura. Their induction into the Indian Police Service is expected to strengthen the senior leadership structure of the state police and enhance its administrative and operational capabilities. The ceremonial event at Police Headquarters marked a proud occasion for the Tripura Police fraternity, highlighting the promotion opportunities available to State Police Service officers and their progression into the country’s premier policing cadre. title: Mibro GS Explorer S Review: 3 Weeks on My Wrist - Dapper and groomed
content: I've tested quite a few smartwatches and health trackers over the years, including the Apple Watch, Kospet smartwatches and, more recently, the RingConn Gen 3 smart ring. And one thing I've learned is that you don't necessarily have to spend a fortune to get a good smartwatch. The Mibro GS Explorer S is a good example. It's a rugged smartwatch designed primarily for outdoor activities, with a ceramic bezel, a beautiful AMOLED display, dual-frequency GPS and over 150 sports modes. But what really caught my attention was the combination of its design, battery life and price. I've always preferred traditional round watches to rectangular ones like the Apple Watch. For me, a smartwatch should still look and feel like a proper watch, and the Explorer S certainly delivers on that front. I've been wearing it for around three weeks. I haven't been climbing mountains or practising extreme sports, but I've used it every day for walking, tracking my health and monitoring my sleep. So, is the Mibro GS Explorer S worth buying, particularly if you don't want to spend Apple Watch money? Here's my experience. I've been using the Mibro GS Explorer S for approximately three weeks, paired with my iPhone 17. I wore it throughout the day and also at night to monitor my sleep. Most of my outdoor activities involved walking my dog, Marlow, exercising and longer countryside walks, including one around the River Severn. I concentrated on the features I would actually use: the display, notifications, health monitoring, GPS, operating system and battery life. For the health tracking, I also wore my RingConn Gen 3 smart ring at the same time. I've tested quite a few health trackers, and the RingConn remains one of my favourites for monitoring everyday health and sleep. I also compared the Mibro's step-counting results with my Apple Watch to see how closely the figures matched. I didn't test all 150-plus sports modes or take the watch diving, so this review focuses on everyday use, walking and the features I've experienced personally. Everything included with the Mibro GS Explorer S, including two interchangeable straps and the magnetic charging cable. I always appreciate a good unboxing experience, particularly when reviewing more affordable technology, and Mibro has done a good job here. The packaging feels premium, and the watch itself makes an excellent first impression. Nothing about the presentation immediately suggests a budget smartwatch. Inside the box, you get the Mibro GS Explorer S, two silicone straps and a magnetic charging cable. I particularly like that Mibro includes two straps, one dark grey and one orange. It's a thoughtful addition because you can change the look of the watch without having to purchase another strap separately. The only thing I'm not particularly keen on is the charging cable. It's a proprietary magnetic connector, which means you need to keep the supplied cable rather than simply using a standard USB-C charging cable. This isn't unusual with smartwatches, but I would prefer a more universal solution. Still, considering the overall presentation and the additional strap, I think Mibro has made a good effort. This is probably my favourite part of the Mibro GS Explorer S. I've always had a preference for traditional round watches, and the Explorer S looks much closer to a rugged sports watch than a piece of technology strapped to your wrist. The watch has a 47.8mm case, a ceramic bezel and a reinforced polymer body, with Corning Gorilla Glass protecting the screen. It's quite a substantial watch, weighing approximately 71g with its silicone strap. I'm not going to pretend this is a particularly light or discreet smartwatch. It's a big, chunky watch, but that's very much part of its design. What surprised me was how comfortable it remained throughout the day. I wore it while working, walking and sleeping, and despite its size, I never found it particularly uncomfortable. The physical buttons also feel good. They have a satisfying click, and I found them easy to operate without having to rely entirely on the touchscreen. It has a resolution of 466 × 466 pixels and a claimed peak brightness of 1,500 nits. In everyday use, it's sharp, colourful and easy to read. More importantly, I had no problems checking the time or other information outdoors, even in bright conditions. I also used the always-on display throughout my testing because that's how I prefer to use a smartwatch. I want to be able to glance at my wrist and see the time without having to make an exaggerated movement to wake the screen. There is one area where I think Mibro could improve, though: the watch faces. You have a selection of different designs available through the Mibro Fit application, but I struggled to find one that really suited my taste. This is obviously personal, and other people might love them. For me, however, many of the designs didn't quite match the attractive, premium appearance of the watch itself. I would have liked a better selection of classic, minimalist watch faces. A closer look at the Explorer S's substantial case and physical buttons, which felt responsive throughout my testing. The Explorer S is designed to withstand more demanding conditions than an ordinary lifestyle smartwatch. Mibro advertises MIL-STD-810H durability testing and 10ATM water resistance, along with a dedicated outdoor exploration mode. That makes it an interesting option for activities such as hiking, swimming and trekking. It also includes features for recreational freediving, with Mibro specifying support for depths of up to 30 metres. I haven't tested its diving capabilities or subjected it to extreme conditions, so I can't personally confirm those claims. What I can say is that the watch feels solid, well assembled and ready for more demanding use than my normal daily walks. A good smartwatch needs good software, and this is another area where the Explorer S impressed me. The watch runs Mibro Galaxy OS 2.0, while the Mibro Fit application manages your health data, settings and connection to your smartphone. I've previously tested the Kospet Tank T4S, and the overall software experience feels quite similar. The interface is straightforward, with clear menus and easy access to the main functions. In fact, in some ways, I find it easier to navigate than Apple's watchOS. That's not to say it's a more advanced operating system. Apple offers a much larger range of applications and deeper integration with the iPhone. But when it comes to finding basic functions quickly, I rather like Mibro's simpler approach. Mibro Galaxy OS 2.0 has a straightforward interface, with quick access to everyday smartwatch and fitness functions. The application recognised the watch without any problems, and throughout my three weeks of testing, I didn't experience any Bluetooth disconnections. That's important because there's nothing more frustrating than discovering that your smartwatch hasn't been syncing properly. The Mibro Fit application is also pleasantly designed and easy to understand. I could check my health information, look at sleep records, review activities and change settings without having to search through complicated menus. The application is available for both iOS and Android, and Mibro also offers connections with services such as Apple Health, Google Fit and Strava. Overall, I think the combination of the watch and the smartphone application works very well. My only real criticism remains the watch-face selection. The application itself is good, but I would like to see more attractive designs added in future updates. This is where I think the Explorer S makes the most sense. Despite its outdoor-focused design, you don't need to be a serious athlete to appreciate what it offers. For my daily routine, I mainly wanted a watch that could tell me the time, show a few important notifications, monitor my activity and last long enough that I didn't have to think about charging it every night. I'm not someone who wants every notification from my smartphone appearing on my wrist. I find constant notifications distracting, particularly when I'm working, so I prefer to keep things simple. I did find message notifications useful, though, especially when I was outdoors and didn't want to take my phone out of my pocket. I tested this once, and the person on the other end could hear me without any problems. Does that mean I want to make regular phone calls from my wrist? Absolutely not. I can see the benefit if you need to answer a quick call when your phone isn't easily accessible, but personally, I would still rather use my smartphone. One feature I particularly enjoyed was the weather application. It's simple, useful and exactly the kind of information I appreciate having available on my wrist before heading outside. At the end of the day, I still see a smartwatch primarily as a watch. Everything else should make everyday life a little easier, not more complicated. This was one of the most interesting parts of my testing. As I mentioned earlier, I've been using the RingConn Gen 3, and after trying numerous health trackers, I consider it one of the more convincing devices I've personally tested for monitoring my everyday health. So I wore both devices simultaneously to see how their results compared. Heart rate: The readings from the Mibro GS Explorer S were very similar to those recorded by my RingConn Gen 3. Blood oxygen: Again, both devices produced closely matching readings during my testing. Sleep tracking: There were some differences between the two, generally around 15 to 20 minutes in the recorded sleep duration. Personally, I don't consider that particularly concerning. Sleep tracking is complicated, and two devices worn on different parts of the body won't necessarily identify the exact same moment when you fall asleep or wake up. I also compared the step count with my Apple Watch, which I've found to be a reliable reference point during my own testing. Would I prefer completely identical results? Of course. But I don't expect that from two different consumer devices using different sensors and algorithms. Before I became a full-time blogger, I worked in pharmacy as a healthcare assistant, and one thing that stuck with me is how easily health tracking can tip into stress. I've seen people become anxious about a single reading, or obsess over a number that was never meant to be a diagnosis. So my advice with any consumer health device, including this one, is to treat the readings as useful information first. They're a guide to your general trends, not a verdict on your health. None of these comparisons proves medical accuracy, and I wouldn't use a smartwatch or smart ring to diagnose a health problem. Where I think the Explorer S is genuinely valuable is on the activity side. The step counts, the heart-rate trends during walks, the GPS routes, the sleep patterns over time — that's the information I found most useful, because it supports the things you're already doing rather than turning health into a project. Use it more for your sports and daily activity, and less as a medical instrument, and I think you'll get the most out of it. In that respect, its health tracking was one of the things that impressed me most. The Mibro GS Explorer S includes dual-frequency L1 and L5 satellite positioning, with support for several global navigation systems. On paper, that's an impressive feature for a smartwatch in this price category. I used the GPS primarily for walking, including a longer route around the River Severn and the surrounding countryside. Once the watch had established its position, I found the tracking to be very accurate. The recorded route matched my walk well, and I didn't notice any major problems during that longer outing. Sometimes the watch takes longer than my iPhone to establish its location. It doesn't happen every time, but it happened often enough for me to notice. For someone like me who mainly uses the watch for walking, this isn't a major problem. I can wait a little longer before starting an activity. But I can imagine how frustrating it might become if you're a regular runner who wants to start recording a workout immediately. Once connected, though, the GPS performed well in the conditions I tested. The watch also offers more than 150 sports modes and additional outdoor tools, including navigation, a compass and altitude information. I didn't explore every sports mode, simply because there are far more than I would ever use. If you're particularly interested in running, cycling, hiking or more specialised outdoor activities, there's certainly plenty to explore. If there's one reason I would seriously consider the Mibro GS Explorer S over an Apple Watch, it's the battery life. Mibro claims up to 20 days of battery life under its specified daily-use conditions. In my own testing, I managed almost two weeks before needing to recharge it. And that's with the always-on display enabled, regular health tracking, notifications and wearing the watch overnight. My Apple Watch needs charging far more frequently, and although I've become used to that, it's quite refreshing to wear a smartwatch without constantly thinking about the battery. The battery life also makes the Explorer S much more practical for sleep tracking. You don't have to plan when to recharge it so that you can wear it overnight. In that respect, the experience reminds me of the RingConn Gen 3, another device I've enjoyed partly because of its long battery life. Of course, if you're using GPS for several hours every day, you should expect shorter battery life than I experienced. But for my combination of daily walking, health monitoring and general smartwatch use, I really couldn't ask for much more. I think this is an interesting comparison because I've spent time with all three devices, and they offer rather different experiences. The Apple Watch remains the more complete smartwatch, particularly if you use an iPhone. It has a more developed software ecosystem, more advanced smart features and a greater range of health-related functions, depending on the model. If health tracking and deep iPhone integration are your priorities, I would still lean towards the Apple Watch. However, there are three things I prefer about the Mibro. First, the design. I genuinely prefer its round, traditional watch appearance. Second, the battery life. Being able to wear it for almost two weeks without charging is a significant advantage over the Apple Watch models I've used. The Explorer S costs considerably less than many Apple Watch models, yet still offers the main functions I use regularly. For someone who wants notifications, step counting, heart-rate monitoring, GPS and a good-looking watch, that difference in price is worth considering. The Mibro GS Explorer S alongside my RingConn Gen 3. I wore both devices during testing to compare heart rate, blood oxygen and sleep-tracking results. Comparing the Explorer S with the RingConn Gen 3 is a little different because they're not really competing to do the same job. The RingConn is a smart ring designed primarily for passive health monitoring. It's discreet, lightweight and particularly comfortable to wear overnight. And I still prefer it if my main interest is understanding my health and sleep patterns over time. But the Mibro offers several advantages that a ring simply cannot provide. You have a large display, GPS tracking, sports modes, notifications, a weather application and the ability to check information directly from your wrist. During my tests, the Mibro also produced heart-rate and blood oxygen readings close to those from the RingConn, while sleep duration varied by around 15 to 20 minutes. So I wouldn't dismiss the Explorer S as a health tracker simply because it costs less. Still, if I were buying a device specifically for long-term health monitoring, I would choose the RingConn Gen 3. If I wanted a proper watch with health monitoring, outdoor features and a much larger range of everyday functions, I would choose the Mibro. In many ways, these two devices complement each other rather well. After three weeks with the Mibro GS Explorer S, I can say that I genuinely enjoyed using it. I love the design, the AMOLED display is beautiful, the operating system is easy to navigate and the battery life is outstanding. The health tracking also performed better than I expected, particularly when compared with my RingConn Gen 3 and Apple Watch. The watch is relatively large and heavy, the selection of watch faces could be better and GPS positioning sometimes takes longer than I would like. But none of those issues seriously affected my everyday experience. If you're a very active person who enjoys hiking, trekking or outdoor sports, the Explorer S is certainly worth looking at, particularly if you want a rugged smartwatch without spending a fortune. And even if you're more like me, someone who enjoys long walks, wants to keep an eye on their health and simply appreciates a good-looking watch, I think there's a lot to like. At the time of writing, Mibro lists the Explorer S for $139.99/£133.99 on its website, reduced from $199.99/£199.99. At that price, I think it represents very good value. It might not replace an Apple Watch for someone who relies heavily on Apple's ecosystem, or a RingConn Gen 3 for someone primarily interested in detailed health monitoring. But as an attractive, durable everyday smartwatch with excellent battery life and useful outdoor features, the Mibro GS Explorer S gets a lot right. And sometimes, that's exactly what you need from a watch. After three weeks with the Mibro GS Explorer S, I found a rugged smartwatch with a superb AMOLED display, impressive health tracking and almost two weeks of battery life. title: BMW GS Experience 2026 Chennai Level 2: Learning to Let It Slide - BikeWale
content: BMW GS Experience 2026 Chennai Level 2 began where the first day had deliberately stopped. The basics were already established. Now the motorcycle was going to be allowed to move more freely on the loose surface. Yes, we were terrified but must soldier on. Around 70 customers turned up for the second day making it noticeably busier than Level 1. There were motorcycles from several generations of BMW's GS family from the G 310 GS through the new F 450 GS and F 900 GS to the R 1250 GS, R 1300 GS and R 1300 GS Adventure. Some motorcycles were conventional manuals. Some of the latest machines brought newer systems such as the Easy Ride Clutch on the F 450 GS and Automated Shift Assistant on boxer-powered models. That made the gathering an interesting mix of how quickly adventure motorcycles themselves are changing. BMW defines Level 2 as its more advanced off-road module with training covering riding position, Enduro Pro, Figure of Eight steering, emergency braking, sand and gravel, off-camber terrain, steep inclines, quick U-turns and slope recovery. We again used the R 1250 GS, but this time selected Enduro Pro. Notably, this single change transformed the purpose of the exercises. Level 1 was largely about learning what the motorcycle could do while its electronics remained ready to protect the rider from some mistakes. Level 2 was about understanding what happens when those systems deliberately move further into the background. This does not mean Enduro Pro turns a GS into an analogue motorcycle. Far from it. What changes is the point at which the systems intervene and, in some cases, whether they intervene at all. And once the rear tyre is allowed to spin and slide more freely, the rider has nowhere to hide poor throttle control. The difference between Enduro and Enduro Pro is one of the most important lessons BMW can teach a GS owner. On the R 1250 GS, Enduro mode is intended for off-road use with road tyres. It hence offers a softer throttle response, recalibrated ABS and traction control permitting some controlled movement while keeping the electronic safety net. BMW specifies it for more serious off-road use with cleated tyres. Throttle response moves from the restrained setting used in Enduro to what BMW calls an optimum response, and the rider can further configure it. When the rear brake pedal is used, ABS regulation at the rear wheel is switched off. Rear-wheel lift detection is also inactive. In its Enduro Pro ABS setting, ABS Pro is not available, while DTC is calibrated to allow substantially more movement because the system assumes the motorcycle is being ridden off-road on suitable tyres. BMW's R 1250 GS manual goes further. In Enduro, DTC already intervenes later to allow extended drifts and short wheelies. In Enduro Pro, front-wheel lift detection is switched off and the motorcycle permits an even broader operating window before electronic control steps in. Before asking somebody to brake-slide an R 1250 GS, the rider needs to know which safety systems remain active. The newer R 1300 GS follows the same philosophy. BMW states that its configurable Enduro Pro mode is meant for rough-tread off-road tyres, with rear-wheel ABS switched off as the factory setting, lift-off detection inactive, later traction-control intervention and engine drag torque control inactive. The new F 450 GS, for example, comes with Rain, Road and Enduro modes as standard, while Riding Modes Pro adds Enduro Pro on higher variants. It also carries ABS Pro, Dynamic Traction Control, Dynamic Brake Control and engine drag torque control. The GS Trophy version adds BMW's Easy Ride Clutch. ERC itself is an interesting development for off-road riding. It uses a centrifugal mechanism to engage the clutch according to engine speed, reducing the need to manually work the clutch during starts and stops. However, these exercises did unveil a few shortcomings of the ERC. There is no bite below 2,700rpm, and that’s where a lot of off-roading happens. ASA takes a different route. BMW's Automated Shift Assistant uses two electromechanical actuators to control the clutch and gear changes in a conventional six-speed transmission. Automatic clutch control can also help during starts on inclines and off-road terrain. But this too is not as good as having full manual control on the clutch, we’re afraid that is irreplaceable. With the system basics understood, the riding became considerably more demanding. Enduro steering returned through a tighter Figure of Eight. It seems like a simple progression from Level 1 until you attempt to repeatedly move a large GS from one lean angle to the other while maintaining balance and momentum. The Figure of Eight forces several inputs to happen together. The rider needs to look through one turn while already preparing for the next. The motorcycle has to lean underneath the body without the rider becoming rigid. Throttle needs to remain stable enough to prevent sudden weight transfer. Steering input has to be deliberate but not aggressive. Do it poorly and every mistake compounds the next one! Emergency braking in Enduro Pro followed, and this was where the electronic difference became easier to feel. Because rear ABS intervention is removed when using the rear brake in the relevant Enduro Pro setting on the R 1250 GS, the rider can deliberately lock the rear wheel. That sounds dramatic until you understand why it is useful. On loose dirt, a sliding rear tyre can be used to help position the motorcycle. This teaches the rider where grip ends than allowing ABS to constantly hide that threshold. Yes, the front brake is more important for outright stopping performance. However, applying it on loose ground requires progressive inputs and extensive knowledge of load transfer. The goal here is to understand what and when the rider must take over when electronics step back. Then came sand and gravel. The front wheel begins moving around and the natural reaction is to hold the bars more tightly. That usually makes matters worse. Training sort of reinforced us to allow some movement instead as the bike needs a measured throttle and enough freedom at the front to carve its path. Rider's legs support the body while the arms remain comparatively relaxed. Vision stays further ahead rather than following every movement of the front tyre, please look ahead. Throttle control is important here as closing it suddenly when the front begins wandering can transfer load forward and make the tyre dig into the soft surface. A continuous input hence helps the motorcycle maintain momentum. Too much active input might turn useful rear-wheel slip into excessive wheelspin and digging holes in the ground. Off-camber riding further introduces gravity from the side into the picture. The bike naturally wants to move downhill, so the rider has to manage line choice, throttle and body position while also avoiding abrupt steering inputs. Riders learn to choose the intended line and keep enough pace to prevent the motorcycle from simply dropping. Long climbs and descents stretch all these techniques over a slightly longer distance. Short climbs can sometimes be handled with momentum even if the technique is not perfect. But the longer ones expose mistakes. Incorrect gear selection, excessive wheelspin or badly placed body weight eventually catches up with the rider. Moving the upper body forward will help manage front-wheel lift here, but don’t forget that traction is still at the rear wheel. Constantly balance weight distribution against grip with a steady throttle because a sudden burst can break traction while an abrupt closure can kill momentum. The long descent demanded almost the opposite approach. The body moves to give the motorcycle room beneath it, arms stay loose and braking is spread over the available grip rather than applied in panic. Engine braking also becomes part of the equation here. This is where the GS Experience begins moving beyond obstacle practice. These are techniques that directly translate to real trails. The quick U-turn was perhaps the best illustration of the difference between Level 2 and Level 1 we did the first morning. Instead of slowly steering the motorcycle through a tight turn, this exercise introduces a controlled brake slide to help rotate the rear of the bike and throttle out quickly with a sharper angle. The rider controls direction and body position. So just dump the clutch and let it spin. Any angle above 90 degrees is going to help you out of a tight spot easily. Level 2 does not make somebody a GS Trophy competitor, nor does participation automatically create a route into the international event. What it does is introduce many of the core abilities that advanced adventure riding demands. Electronics can create a wider margin. Skill decides how that margin is used. After two days in Chennai, that became our main takeaway from the BMW GS Experience 2026. Level 1 showed us how much easier a big GS becomes when the rider stops fighting it. Level 2 showed the other side of the equation. Once the electronics give you more freedom, the motorcycle also gives you fewer excuses.

, the Wall Street firm best known for its trading desks and deal advisory work, used its quarterly earnings call last month to put the spotlight on a less glamorous but increasingly important line of business: financing. According to a summary of the call published by Zacks, executives highlighted growth in the firm's financing activities while also discussing the uncertainty that artificial intelligence creates for the business. The update keeps Goldman Sachs firmly on the radar of investors tracking Financial Stocks. The financing push sits at the heart of the strategy Chief Executive David Solomon has pursued for several years. By lending to hedge funds, asset managers and corporate clients through prime brokerage, repo and structured lending, the firm aims to generate revenue that is less dependent on volatile trading volumes or the timing of large mergers. Shares of Goldman Sachs trade on the New York Stock Exchange, which places the stock in the NYSE Composite, and it is also a constituent of the S&P 500, the [Dow Jones Industrial Average] and the Russell 1000. Earnings summaries compiled by Quartr captured the broad shape of the quarter for the market. The Zacks summary of the call singled out financing growth as among its central themes. In Goldman Sachs's reporting, financing revenue appears within its trading businesses in both FICC and equities, capturing the fees and spreads the firm earns by extending credit and balance-sheet capacity to clients. Prime brokerage is a bundle of services that large banks offer hedge funds. The prime broker lends money so the fund can amplify its positions, lends out securities the fund wants to bet against, clears and settles trades, and safeguards the collateral that secures those loans. The bank earns spreads on the lending and fees on the services, and the size of the business tends to move with the total value of client portfolios. Historically, Goldman Sachs earned a large share of its revenue from activities that rise and fall sharply with markets, including trading, underwriting, merger advice and principal stakes in companies. That model delivered strong results in good years but left the firm exposed in downturns, and the market tended to value its earnings at a discount to more consistent banks. The Zacks summary described AI as a topic of concern on the call, framing it alongside the financing story. While the precise remarks are not reproduced here, Wall Street executives have generally pointed to several areas where AI introduces uncertainty: cybersecurity and fraud, model errors, data protection and the speed at which competitors can adopt new tools. Goldman Sachs has publicly described an initiative to reorganize how the firm works around artificial intelligence, reviewing processes from client onboarding to lending operations and regulatory reporting. The firm has said it aims to use the technology to automate repetitive tasks and free staff for higher-value work. Goldman Sachs is far from alone in prizing financing revenue. Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase and the large European dealers have all expanded prime brokerage and related lending as hedge funds and other institutional clients have grown. The contest for these relationships is intense, and clients often spread their business across several providers to diversify counterparty exposure. Goldman Sachs remains among the top-ranked advisers on global mergers and acquisitions, and its fees from advising on deals and underwriting stock and bond offerings are a major driver of results. Deal activity has been recovering after a prolonged slowdown earlier in the decade, helped by more stable markets and renewed corporate confidence. The firm's next scheduled earnings release covers final-quarter and full year and is typically issued in mid-January. That report will show whether financing revenue sustained its momentum and will likely include further commentary on AI-driven efficiency efforts. Ever since West Geauga’s Ian Res ended the 2025 Ohio High School Athletic Association Division II state meet with a sixth-place finish, his goal was to become a state champion. He completed that goal on Saturday, Nov. 7, becoming the first state champion in West Geauga history to win the cross-country state title. So, doing things that him and Danny [Kearns] never did is definitely big.” Last year’s sixth-place finish was a big learning point that Res used this year and allowed him to capture the crown. “Last year I didn’t put myself in it enough,” Res said. “I think if I did, I could have placed a little bit higher. So, this year I just wanted to make sure I ran my own race and didn’t let other guys dictate it and their game plan and just kind of tried to control it more. Like the kid that went out in front with a big lead for the first mile-and-a-half, just being a senior and having the confidence to know that he probably wasn’t going to hold that. A year ago I might have panicked a little bit and tried to bridge that gap a little more and maybe burn myself out.” It was the goal he has been chasing and wanted to accomplish, but doing so in his senior season made the moment even more sweet. “Including track, the last two state championships, indoor and outdoor, I ran in, I got second,” Res said. “Both of those were definitely ones I wanted to win, definitely really thought I could win. So, finally getting one, it was so much sweeter than if I had won one before and this was my second or third. I’m glad that this was my first just because it felt like my work was a lot more worth it.” The title has given him confidence but also a feeling of relief. He has the opportunity to chase two more state titles in the 1600-meter race. “There was more of a relief than anything to win,” Res said. “I feel like I’ve already done the thing that I really wanted to do in high school. title: FC Seoul Champions Energize GS Caltex's V-League Title Bid - 조선일보
content: Sister clubs share championship momentum as FC Seoul returns support after GS Caltex's undefeated 2025-2026 title win [OSEN=Cho Hyung-rae Reporter] GS Caltex Seoul Kixx Volleyball Team (hereinafter GS Caltex) will welcome special guests to their home game against SOOP Super at Jangchung Gymnasium on Saturday, November 14. The FC Seoul squad, including head coach Kim Ki-dong and captain Kim Jin-su, who led the sister club to the 2026 K League 1 title, will visit Jangchung Gymnasium to inject powerful championship energy into GS Caltex’s pursuit of a second consecutive V-League title in the 2026-2027 season. This event carries a special meaning of a "virtuous cycle of victory" between the two clubs. In April, the GS Caltex squad, which achieved a historic undefeated championship run in the 2025-2026 V-League postseason, visited Seoul World Cup Stadium to perform a ceremonial kickoff, passing on their winning momentum to FC Seoul. Having received GS Caltex’s energy, FC Seoul claimed the K League 1 title for the first time in 10 years, lifting the championship trophy. Now, the K League 1 champions will return the favor by bringing their championship energy to Jangchung Gymnasium, aiming to fuel GS Caltex’s bid for a second consecutive V-League title. Before the match, FC Seoul’s head coach Kim Ki-dong and captain Kim Jin-su, who led the team to the K League 1 title, will participate in the ceremonial first pitch to energize the atmosphere at Jangchung Gymnasium. The FC Seoul players in the stands will also cheer fervently for the GS Caltex athletes, showcasing the strong championship DNA shared between the sister clubs of GS Sports. GS Caltex captain Yu Seo-yeon said, "Last spring, we were proud and delighted as sister clubs when FC Seoul claimed the K League 1 title after 10 years, having received the undefeated championship energy we passed on. This time, we will carry forward the hot energy of the champions delivered by FC Seoul and, together with our fans, run fiercely until the end to achieve a second consecutive V-League title in the 2026-2027 season."

title: Choi Ga-eun's 11 Points, 3 Blocks Lead GS Caltex Victory - 조선일보
content: Overcoming injuries, star player propels team to 3-0 win against Suwon Hyundai Engineering & Construction [Suwon = Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] In her 8th year since debut, her 4th team. Choi Ga-eun has firmly established herself as a cornerstone of GS Caltex. Choi Ga-eun recorded 11 points and 3 blocks in the match against Suwon Hyundai Engineering & Construction on the 11th, leading her team to a 3-0 victory. After the game, Choi Ga-eun smiled and said, "Today, my reception was good, so I was able to perform well." She added, "During the offseason, I focused on developing various attack routes and prepared diligently. Even during counterattacks, I continued to attempt quick attacks and central attacks in difficult situations." Now in her 8th season since debut, she has experienced half of the league. Choi Ga-eun, who was selected 5th overall in the 1st round by Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK) in 2019, later played for Pepper Savings Bank and Korea Expressway Corporation before joining GS Caltex in 2024. Earlier, GS Caltex manager Lee Young-taek praised Choi Ga-eun's growth: "She couldn't play much for a while due to injuries, but since the second half of last season, her increased playing time helped her regain confidence. Her quick attack chemistry with setter Kim Ji-won is truly excellent." Choi Ga-eun said, "I now have close friends on every team. My outgoing personality made adapting easy." However, she also shared, "At Pepper Savings Bank, which was a newly founded team, we built everything from scratch, and I enjoyed getting a lot of playing time. Those experiences were invaluable." "At GS Caltex, shoulder injuries were a problem. Since the second half of last season, the manager gave me opportunities, and my performance steadily improved. Winning the championship last season gave me great pride. I prepared for this season with that confidence." On this day, GS Caltex dominated with strong serves and team blocking (11-4). With Choi Ga-eun's central attacks revitalized, the offensive burden on the trio of Silva (20 points), Tanacha (12 points), and Kwon Min-ji (11 points) decreased. This marked a clear contrast from last season, when Silva scored 41 points but still lost (February 16 match against Hyundai Engineering & Construction). Choi Ga-eun explained, "The strategy analysis system has been slightly updated. It's great that players can directly watch and analyze videos. We watched a lot of opponent footage before each game, and our preparation worked well. Today, our serve strategy was effective, making it easier to read the opponent's attacks. Thanks to that, my blocking form was good, and there were almost no dropped balls after contact." GS Caltex's strength lies in its lively and passionate team atmosphere centered around Silva and Kwon Min-ji. This year, with Tanacha joining, the team gained even more momentum. Manager Lee Young-taek smiled and said, "Tanacha is a player with a strong desire for volleyball. She creates great synergy in both offense and defense." Choi Ga-eun added, "I also perform better when I'm in a lively mood." "After enduring long injuries, my goal this season is to play in every match. I want to finish the season without injuries. This season, I hope to show many moments of a lively Choi Ga-eun." Suwon = Kim Young-rok Reporter lunarfly@sportschosun.com

They were really good lads; to me, they were almost like my own sons.” Between 1970 and 1981, Schneider’s GS Team was regarded as a fixture in German motor racing. Touring car stars such as Dieter Basche, Hans-Joachim Stuck, Albrecht Krebs and Jörg Obermoser claimed victories in the BMW 2002 and 320 models from the Freiburg-based tuning workshop. Stuck and Nelson Piquet even won the 1,000 km race at the Nürburgring in 1981 in a GS-BMW M 1 prototype. Schneider pulled off what was arguably his greatest coup with the surprise Lancia deal for Hans Heyer, who had been driving for Ford for many years up to that point. Because Heyer had been annoyed that it was not he, but of all people his close friend and Ford returnee Klaus Ludwig, who had been awarded the drive in the new Super Capri for the 1980 DRM, Heyer and his mate Domingis Piedade hatched the Lancia plan. Piedade, who had an excellent international network and was also team manager at GS Sport, brokered the deal with the Italians, with the result that Heyer won the 1980 DRM in the Lancia Beta Turbo – and did so just ahead of Klaus Ludwig. For Schneider and his GS Sport team, this was undoubtedly one of their most significant successes ever. And yet, from 1981 onwards, despite a solid base of sponsors such as BASF, Warsteiner and Jägermeister, Schneider’s racing team and business empire began to go into decline. The BMW dealership, including the racing team and tuning business, the car hire firm, the distribution of Winnebago luxury motorhomes and the Fruit of the Loom sportswear mail order business all had to be given up one after the other due to financial difficulties. Schneider suddenly found himself facing a huge shambles. Frustrated and disappointed, he disappeared to Turkey. Even his closest associates, such as Mario Ketterer from Freiburg, had no idea for years where the former racing team owner and then-chairman of the FC Freiburg football club was. It was only after many years that the former racing team boss returned to Germany and took stock, with a degree of self-criticism: “Yes, I made mistakes that led to the collapse of my group of companies. But I was also too trusting for the cut-throat world of motor racing; in the end, I was shamelessly exploited. I paid a high price for my willingness to help and my good nature.” The well over 100 victories achieved by his cars and drivers were just as much a thing of the past for him as motor racing itself. In a telephone conversation in 2002, Schneider had told me bitterly: “I now know how I must shape the rest of my life – anything to do with cars is most certainly no longer part of it.” Twenty years later, on 11 August 2022, Gerhard Schneider died at the age of 86. He would have turned 90 in 2026. title: GS E&C Opens "Areumyuje Xi" Sales Showroom on Nov. 12 - 아시아경제
content:
GS E&C Opens "Areumyuje Xi" Sales Showroom on Nov. 12 GS E&C announced on November 12 that it would open a sales showroom for Areumyuje Xi in the area around 586 Seongpo-dong, Sangnok-gu, Ansan, Gyeonggi-do, and begin full-scale sales. A bird's-eye view of Armuje Xi, planned for the area around 586 Seongpo-dong, Sangnok-gu, Ansan, Gyeonggi-do. GS E&C Areumyuje Xi will comprise six buildings, with six basement levels and 49 above-ground floors: four apartment buildings and two officetel buildings, offering a total of 1,354 homes, including 984 apartments and 370 officetel units. Of the total, the 984 apartments will mainly consist of mid- to large-sized units with exclusive areas of 84, 99, and 104 m². The complex name, "ARMUSEE," combines "ART" with the French word "MUSEE," meaning an art museum. It reflects the aim of creating a residential culture that goes beyond simply providing a place to live, curating art, personal tastes, and experiences in everyday life. Applications will be submitted through the Korea Real Estate Board's Cheongyak Home website, with special-supply applications opening on November 23, followed by first-priority applications on November 24 and second-priority applications on November 25. The winners will be announced on December 1, and formal contracts will be signed over three days, from December 13 to 15. Applicants must be at least 19 years old as of the date of the public notice for the housing offering, have held a housing subscription savings account for at least 12 months, and meet the deposit requirements for their region and unit size. Ansan residents may apply under the local-area category, while residents of other parts of Gyeonggi-do, Seoul, and Incheon may apply under the other-area category. If there is competition, Ansan residents applying under the local-area category will receive priority. Household members who are not the head of the household may also apply. Homeowners may apply for first-priority status regardless of how many homes they own, and there is no restriction on winning again. Winners of 84 m² units will be selected through a points-based system for 40% of the units and a lottery for 60%. All 99 m² and 104 m² units, which exceed 85 m², will be allocated by lottery. The down payment will be reduced to 5% of the contract price, and interest on interim payments will be deferred until later. Free balcony extensions will also be offered to reduce buyers' initial costs. The resale restriction will last six months from the date the winners are announced. Areumyuje Xi is located where residents can enjoy access to both the Seongpo-dong and Jungang-dong neighborhoods, and is close to Jungang Station, served by Line 4 and the Suin-Bundang Line. Full-scale construction on the GTX-C line, which will include Ansan's Sangnoksu Station as a stop, began last September. Nearby amenities include major retailers such as Lotte Department Store, Lotte Mart, and NC Department Store, as well as cultural and medical facilities such as CGV and Korea University Ansan Hospital. Green spaces are also close by. The floor plans are designed to make the most of the space to meet demand for larger homes. The 84 m² A type features a dining area with a view, separate from the kitchen, and an additional room. The 99 m² A type has four bedrooms and a wide dining area. The 104 m² type has three bedrooms, an additional room, and a beta room. Key unit types also include ample storage, with large dressing rooms, pantries, utility rooms, and entrance storage closets. A "Water Terrace," combining water features and gardens, will be created at ground level, giving residents convenient access to water and greenery within the complex. Art sculptures will be placed throughout the grounds. Other amenities will include a "Sound Chamber," a space for enjoying music and video on a large screen with immersive sound; a 49th-floor sky lounge; a sky guesthouse; and a private dining room (PDR). The complex will also have a fitness center, a GX room, a Pilates room, an indoor golf practice facility equipped with a putting simulator, and a sauna. Plans are also under consideration for a "Xi Wellness Lounge" for healthcare, a small library within the complex, a private storage service, Open Gallery, an art subscription platform, and community dining services. The Areumyuje Xi sales showroom will be located at 719-7 Gojan-dong, Danwon-gu, Ansan, Gyeonggi-do. The complex is scheduled for completion in the first half of 2031. © The Asia Business Daily. title: GS E&C in Talks With KDB as Battery Unit Nears Default - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Energy Materials Halted Pohang Plant Last Month Amid Losses
KDB Can Demand Immediate Repayment of 112.5 Billion Won
Cross-Default Clause Prompts GS E&C to Shift Course GS E&C (006360) has opened talks with the Korea Development Bank to resolve loans owed by Energy Materials, its battery recycling unit now facing default. The trigger is a cross-default clause that could force early repayment of the parent company's foreign-currency bonds if the subsidiary fails to meet its obligations. GS E&C, which had cut off further funding to the unit, is seeking a way to keep the credit risk from spreading to the parent. GS E&C recently began discussions with KDB over 112.5 billion won ($77 million) in outstanding loans owed by Energy Materials, according to industry sources on the 11th. "Simply declaring default would be reckless as a way of running a business," a GS E&C official said. "We will sort this out internally so that it does not happen." A KDB official said the bank is "in discussions to resolve this amicably with GS." Energy Materials, founded in 2020, is 77.65% owned by GS E&C. The company extracts nickel, cobalt and lithium from spent batteries. KDB approved a 120 billion won loan in 2022 to fund construction of the Pohang plant, and Energy Materials had been servicing the principal and interest with money borrowed from GS E&C. But as the slowdown in the electric vehicle market made raw material procurement difficult and plant utilization stalled at around 30%, the Pohang plant suspended operations on the 28th of last month. KDB sent a notice of pending event of default the following day. An EOD allows a lender to demand repayment of the entire loan at once before maturity. That gives KDB the right to claim the full 112.5 billion won balance, effectively the authority to put Energy Materials into default. GS E&C has so far refused to repay the debt directly. The company cites legal risks, including breach of fiduciary duty, if a parent repays debt on behalf of a separate legal entity in the absence of a payment guarantee or debt assumption agreement. An accounting firm review projecting prolonged losses ahead also factored into the decision. Last month, GS E&C stopped extending additional loans to the unit. The cross-default clause emerged as a variable in the process. Foreign-currency bonds worth $30 million, issued by GS E&C headquarters in March last year, carry a clause under which failure by a subsidiary to meet its debt obligations also creates grounds for early redemption of those bonds. If the EOD on the Energy Materials loan is confirmed, an EOD could also arise on the parent company's bonds on or around the 12th. At roughly 40 billion won, the foreign-currency bonds are not an unmanageable amount, but losing the benefit of maturity on parent company bonds because of a subsidiary's troubles could damage GS E&C's credit standing. Financial investment industry observers see the most likely outcome as banks holding the bonds agreeing, after KDB confirms the Energy Materials EOD, to waive application of the cross-default clause. GS E&C has provided a total of 155.9 billion won to Energy Materials to date, including 127 billion won through a rights offering and 28.9 billion won in loans. But as business conditions deteriorated, Energy Materials' net loss widened to 90.9 billion won last year from 32.7 billion won in 2024, and GS E&C booked an 79.9 billion won impairment loss on its stake in the unit last year. Cumulative losses total about 170 billion won. GS E&C put the unit up for sale in August last year but failed to find a buyer. After halting additional loans last month, Energy Materials is now accepting voluntary retirement applications from its roughly 130 employees. The company plans to revive the sale once restructuring is complete. Original reporting by Woo Young-tak for Seoul Economic Daily. AI-translated from Korean. title: Ministry of Science and ICT Mandates GS Engineering & Construction Hack Probe - 조선일보
content: The Ministry of Science and ICT has launched a mandatory investigation into a hacking incident that occurred in GS Engineering & Construction’s apartment community facility reservation and management system. This marks the first case where the newly established “Intrusion Accident Investigation Deliberation Committee” conducted a mandatory investigation following its review last month. The Ministry of Science and ICT announced on the 11th, “GS Engineering & Construction reported the intrusion incident on the 29th of last month but declined to agree to a Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) investigation, opting to analyze the incident internally.” However, the committee concluded that a mandatory investigation was necessary, considering the scale of the data leak and the sensitivity of the information involved. The committee is a statutory body established to proactively respond to intrusion incidents. Earlier, GS Engineering & Construction confirmed unauthorized external access to its apartment community facility reservation and management system around 10:15 p.m. on October 28 and reported the incident to KISA the following day. The potentially leaked information includes residents’ names, birthdates, mobile phone numbers, genders, email addresses, addresses, passwords, membership numbers, residence types, and whether they are household heads. Administrator IDs, final login IP addresses, and RF card numbers were also among the potentially compromised data. A source from GS Engineering & Construction stated, “The company did not refuse the government and KISA’s investigation but only declined technical support for internal cause analysis and preventive measures.” They added, “We will fully cooperate with ongoing investigations, including KISA’s.”

title: Want to invest in government bonds? RBI's 6.94% GS 2036 auction opens on November 13: How to apply - Upstox
content: 3 min read | Updated on November 11, 2026, 09:57 IST RBI will auction its 6.94% GS 2036 bond on November 13. Find out how retail investors can apply through RBI Retail Direct, minimum investment and key details. Government of India securities carry no domestic currency credit risk, according to the RBI, but they are subject to market risk. | Image: Shutterstock. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will auction the 6.94% Government of India Security 2036 on November 13, 2026. The government plans to raise ₹34,000 crore through the re-issue, with an option to accept an additional subscription of up to ₹2,000 crore. Individual investors can participate through the non-competitive bidding facility on the RBI Retail Direct platform, with a minimum investment of ₹10,000 in face value. The 6.94% GS 2036 will mature on May 11, 2036. Since this is a re-issue, the auction will be price-based and follow the multiple-price method. Maximum investment: ₹2 crore per investor per security per auction Non-competitive bidding window: 10:30 am to 11:00 am Unlike competitive bidders, retail investors do not have to quote a price or yield. They simply specify the face value they wish to purchase. Allotment takes place at the weighted average price emerging from successful competitive bids. The RBI has provided for up to 5% of the notified amount to be allotted to eligible individuals and institutions under this facility. For this auction, that works out to ₹1,700 crore. After opening the account, they can select the eligible security and submit their non-competitive bid during the specified window on November 13. The minimum bid is ₹10,000 in face value, in multiples of ₹10,000 thereafter. The maximum bid is ₹2 crore per investor per security per auction. The actual payment may differ from the face value because the RBI's calculation includes the indicative price, accrued interest and applicable markup. Not necessarily. The 6.94% is the annual coupon rate, not the actual investment yield. For a face value of ₹10,000, the annual coupon interest is ₹694, generally payable in two instalments of ₹347 each, on May 11 and November 11. The actual yield depends on the auction price. title: GS E&C Opens Talks With Lenders Over Subsidiary's Default Risk - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Battery Recycler Energy Materials Suspends Plant Amid Losses
State Lender Can Demand Immediate Repayment of 112.5 Billion Won
Cross-Default Clause Prompts GS E&C to Reverse Course According to industry sources on Nov. 11, GS E&C recently opened discussions with Korea Development Bank over 112.5 billion won in outstanding loans owed to the bank by Energy Materials, its battery-recycling subsidiary. "Declaring a default without thought would be reckless from a corporate management standpoint," a GS E&C official said. "We will sort this out internally so that doesn't happen." A KDB official also said, "We are in discussions to resolve the matter amicably with GS." Established in 2020, Energy Materials is 77.65% owned by GS E&C. It extracts nickel, cobalt and lithium from spent batteries. KDB approved a 120 billion won loan in 2022 to fund construction of a plant in Pohang, and Energy Materials has been servicing the principal and interest with money borrowed from GS E&C. But as the slowdown in the electric-vehicle market made raw materials harder to secure and the plant's utilization rate stalled at around 30%, the Pohang facility suspended operations on Oct. 28. KDB sent a notice of pending events of default (EOD) the following day. An EOD allows a lender to demand immediate repayment of borrowed funds before maturity. That means KDB can call the entire 112.5 billion won outstanding, effectively giving it the power to put Energy Materials into default. GS E&C has so far refused to repay the debt directly. It argues that Energy Materials is a separate legal entity and that, absent a payment guarantee or debt-assumption agreement, a parent company repaying the debt on its behalf would carry legal risks such as breach of fiduciary duty. An accounting firm's review projecting prolonged losses ahead also factored into the decision. Last month, GS E&C halted additional lending to the unit. The cross-default clause then emerged as a wild card. A $30 million foreign-currency bond issued by GS E&C's parent entity in March last year carries a clause triggering early redemption if a subsidiary fails to meet its obligations. If the EOD on the Energy Materials loan is confirmed, an EOD could also arise on the parent company's bond around Nov. 12. At roughly 40 billion won, the foreign-currency bond is not an unmanageable sum, but losing the benefit of maturity on parent-company debt because of a subsidiary's troubles could damage GS E&C's credit standing. The financial investment industry sees it as most likely that, after KDB confirms the Energy Materials EOD, the banks holding the bond will consult and grant a waiver on applying the cross-default clause. GS E&C had aggressively nurtured Energy Materials as a new business, providing a total of 155.9 billion won, including 127 billion won through rights offerings and 28.9 billion won in loans. But as conditions deteriorated, Energy Materials' net loss widened to 90.9 billion won last year from 32.7 billion won in 2024, and GS E&C booked an 79.9 billion won impairment loss on its stake last year. Cumulative losses total about 170 billion won. GS E&C put the unit up for sale in August last year but failed to find a buyer. After cutting off additional lending last month, Energy Materials is now accepting voluntary retirement applications from its roughly 130 employees. The company plans to revive the sale once restructuring is complete. Original reporting by Woo Young-tak for Seoul Economic Daily. AI-translated from Korean. title: GS, POSCO Join Forces on Large-Scale AI Data Centers - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
■ Deeper Cooperation in Infrastructure and Materials Technology
Stable Supply Chains to Shorten Construction Timelines
Both Companies to Tap Overseas Bases to Expand Business GS Group (078930) and POSCO are forming a strategic partnership to target the fast-growing market for artificial intelligence data center infrastructure. The two aim to combine GS's infrastructure capabilities with POSCO's steel materials technology to meet surging global demand for AI data centers. The companies signed a memorandum of understanding on strategic cooperation in the AI data center business on the 11th at GS Tower in Seoul's Gangnam District. About 10 key officials attended the ceremony, including GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki and POSCO President Lee Hee-keun. The agreement centers on creating synergies by pairing GS Group's data center construction and operation capabilities and global network with POSCO's high-quality steel materials and technology solutions. Specifically, the two companies agreed to jointly identify solutions that strengthen the long-term operational competitiveness of data centers by linking high-efficiency steel materials with design and cooling technologies tailored to data centers. The targeted gains include lower operating costs, better space efficiency and improved durability of equipment and materials. The companies also plan to use the overseas business networks of GS Global (001250) and POSCO to identify global AI data center development demand early, and to jointly pursue supply of materials and equipment for overseas projects along with related business opportunities. Following the agreement, the two sides will set up a group-level working committee to flesh out detailed cooperation tasks, including building an equipment supply chain, developing technologies and solutions, and jointly addressing overseas projects. GS Group is pushing to build a large-scale AI data center in the Bukpyeong No. 2 General Industrial Complex in Donghae, Gangwon State, led by GS AI Infra, a company dedicated to AI data centers. It plans to complete 1.2 gigawatts of capacity in phases starting in 2028 and to secure an additional 1.2 gigawatts, expanding the total to 2.4 gigawatts. The plan is to maximize synergies by drawing on its power and energy capabilities along with the business foundations of affiliates including GS E&C (006360) for design and construction, GS Caltex for liquid cooling and GS Global for overseas networks. POSCO has designated AI data centers as a key area that will drive future steel demand and is strengthening its capabilities in the business. After setting up a future demand development office this year to find demand in new industries such as AI data centers and power grids, it has been expanding development of high value-added steel materials and solutions ranging from structural materials for data center buildings to equipment for power and cooling systems. title: GS, POSCO join hands for future large-scale AI data center projects - The Korea Times
content: GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki, right, poses with POSCO CEO Lee Hee-geun after signing a memorandum of understanding on the two sides' cooperation in the artificial intelligence data center sector at GS Tower in Gangnam District, Seoul, Wednesday. Courtesy of GS Group GS Group and POSCO will form a strategic partnership in the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market, combining GS Group's expertise in data center construction and operation with POSCO's high-quality steel materials and technological solutions. GS Group said Wednesday that it has signed a memorandum of understanding with POSCO on a strategic partnership in the AI data center business. The signing ceremony was attended by GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki, POSCO CEO Lee Hee-geun and other executives from both companies. Through the agreement, the two companies plan to minimize delays in the supply of equipment and materials during the construction of large-scale data centers and optimize material selection and design solutions to shorten construction periods and reduce costs. These efforts are expected to facilitate the early operation of data centers and improve their profitability, GS Group said. The agreement also includes practical cooperation to explore ways to reduce operating costs, improve space utilization and enhance the durability of facilities and equipment to strengthen the long-term operational competitiveness of data centers. The two sides will join efforts for global market entry as well, by leveraging the overseas business networks of GS Global and POSCO to identify data center development demands and jointly explore opportunities to supply materials and equipment for overseas projects. “AI data centers require capabilities from various industries to enable stable power supply, rapid construction and efficient operation,” Hong said. “Through this partnership, we will combine GS Group’s data center development capabilities with POSCO’s world-class materials and solutions to explore new growth opportunities in the global AI infrastructure market.” Lee said AI data centers represent a new growth segment that will drive global demand for steel and materials, adding that the two sides will “establish a strong leadership position in the global AI data center market.” GS Group is currently pursuing a 2.4-gigawatt data center project in Donghae, Gangwon Province, through its subsidiary GS AI Infrastructure. In September, the group announced plans to invest approximately 15 trillion won ($11.23 billion) in the first phase of the project and obtained a construction permit for its first 100-megawatt data center in October. POSCO established a new Future Demand Development Office this year to identify business opportunities in AI data center and power grid businesses. The company is also expanding its development of high-value-added steel materials and solutions for data center applications, ranging from structural components to power and cooling equipment. title: GS Group, POSCO Form 'AI Data Center' Alliance to Target North American and Asian Markets - 아시아경제
content:
GS Group, POSCO Form 'AI Data Center' Alliance to Target North American and Asian Markets GS Group and POSCO have joined forces to tap the artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) market. The two companies plan to combine GS Group's capabilities in building and operating data centers with POSCO's steel materials technology to reduce construction time and costs and expand their business into overseas markets, including North America and Asia. GS Group and POSCO said on the 11th that they had signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on strategic cooperation in the AIDC business at GS Tower in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. About 10 key officials from the two companies attended the signing ceremony, including GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Sunki and POSCO President Lee Heegeun. POSCO President Lee Heegeun (left) and GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Sungi pose for a commemorative photo at a signing ceremony for an MOU on cooperation in the AI data center business at GS Tower in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, on the 11th. GS Group Under the agreement, GS Group will oversee the entire process of developing and operating data center infrastructure, including business planning, power supply, design and construction, and liquid cooling. POSCO will provide steel materials and customized solutions needed to build data centers. The two companies plan to minimize delays in equipment supply and optimize designs and materials to shorten construction periods and reduce costs. GS Group is building a large-scale data center at the Bukpyeong 2nd General Industrial Complex in Donghae, Gangwon Province, through its dedicated subsidiary, GS AI Infra. It plans to complete the facility in phases starting in 2028, with capacity of 1.2 GW, and add a further 1.2 GW in the future to bring the total to 2.4 GW. In September, it announced plans to invest about 15 trillion won in the first phase of the project, and last month it obtained a building permit for its first 100 MW-class data center. GS Group plans to draw on its capabilities in power generation and energy, including GS E&C's design and construction expertise and GS Caltex's liquid-cooling technology, for its data center business. It will also leverage GS Global's overseas network to expand its global operations. POSCO plans to adopt an "EVI (Early Vendor Involvement)" model, moving beyond the conventional approach of supplying steel after data center designs are complete and participating from the initial design stage. It aims to shorten construction periods by recommending steel specifications suited to structures and equipment, reviewing processing methods and performance, and supplying materials in line with construction schedules. Data center construction is expected to use POSCO's PosMAC, a highly corrosion-resistant alloy-coated steel sheet, as well as electromagnetic shielding materials and high-efficiency electrical steel. PosMAC will be used in building interior and exterior materials and cable trays to reduce corrosion and improve durability. Electromagnetic shielding materials will help reduce electromagnetic interference in information technology (IT) equipment such as servers, while high-efficiency electrical steel will be used to improve the energy efficiency of transformers and generators. This year, POSCO established a Future Demand Development Office to identify steel demand in emerging industries, including data centers and power grids. It is also considering ways to apply to data center operations the large-scale power generation and heating and cooling efficiency technologies it has developed through operating steel mills. The two companies plan to expand their business overseas after securing results through cooperation on large-scale domestic data center projects. They will jointly target markets in North America and Asia by leveraging POSCO's global steel supply chain and GS Global's overseas network. To this end, they will establish a working-level council to develop plans for building equipment supply chains, advancing technology, and jointly responding to overseas projects. GS Group Vice Chairman Hong Sunki said, "AI data centers are an area that requires the combined capabilities of various industries to ensure a stable power supply, rapid construction, and efficient operation. Through this cooperation, we will strengthen our business competitiveness and identify new growth opportunities in the global AI infrastructure market." POSCO President Lee Heegeun said, "The rapidly growing AI data center market is a key market of the future that will drive new global demand for steel and materials. By combining POSCO's next-generation steel solutions and design support capabilities with GS Group's infrastructure value chain, we will secure a firm leading position in the global AIDC market." © The Asia Business Daily.
