POSCO and GS join forces on AI data centers, construction and overseas projects Updated
Nov 11, 2026,
4:55 p.m. KST


Published
Nov 11, 2026,
4:30 p.m. KST POSCO and GS Group said Wednesday that they have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) for cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI) data center projects. The signing ceremony was held at the GS Tower in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, on the same day. Hong Soon-ki, Vice Chairman of GS Group, Lee Hee-geun, President of POSCO, and approximately 10 other officials from both companies attended the event. The two companies agreed to cooperate in data center construction and operation, as well as overseas business expansion. Under the agreement, they will combine GS Group’s capabilities in building and operating data centers with POSCO’s steel materials and technology solutions. The plan is to ensure a stable supply of equipment and materials needed for data center construction and to optimize materials and design to reduce construction periods and costs. They are also considering linking high-efficiency steel materials with specialized design and cooling technologies tailored for data centers. GS Group will oversee the entire process of building and operating AI infrastructure, including project planning, power supply, design and construction (GS Construction), and liquid cooling (GS Caltex). Based on its world-class steel technology and stable material supply capabilities, POSCO will maximize the construction stability and profitability of the projects. The companies will also expand cooperation in overseas markets. Leveraging the overseas business networks of GS Global and POSCO, they plan to identify data center development demand and seek opportunities for supplying materials and equipment. The two companies will form a working-level consultation body to concretize plans for building supply chains, developing technology, and jointly responding to overseas projects. POSCO is actively expanding its business scope as an "AI Data Center Total Solution Company." In particular, it has decided to pursue the application of the EVI (Early Vendor Involvement) model, which provides customized steel solutions from the initial stage of a project, moving beyond the conventional method of supplying steel after design drawings are finalized. To shorten construction periods and maximize operational efficiency, POSCO plans to apply specialized materials optimized for AI data center architecture and equipment operation, including PosMAC, electromagnetic interference (shielding) materials, and high-efficiency electrical steel sheets. GS Group is pushing forward with the construction of a large-scale AI data center in the Bukpyeong 2nd General Industrial Complex in Donghae City, Gangwon Province, through its dedicated subsidiary, GS AI Infrastructure. It plans to complete facilities totaling 1.2 gigawatts (GW) in phases starting from 2028 and subsequently secure an additional 1.2 GW, expanding the total capacity to 2.4 GW. In September, the company announced it would invest approximately 1.5 trillion won in the first phase of the project, and in October, it received construction permits for its first 100-megawatt (MW) class data center. Hong Soon-ki, Vice Chairman of GS Group, stated, "By combining GS Group’s data center development capabilities with POSCO’s competitiveness in steel materials and solutions, we will enhance project competitiveness and uncover new growth opportunities in the global AI infrastructure market." Lee Hee-geun, president of POSCO, said, "The explosively growing AI data center sector is a key future market that will newly drive global demand for steel and materials," adding, "By combining GS Group’s infrastructure value chain with POSCO’s next-generation steel solution capabilities, we will secure a firm leading position in the global AI data center market." GS E&C Maintains "Highest" Rating in Win-Win Growth Index for Sixth Consecutive Year GS E&C announced on November 11 that it had maintained the highest rating for the sixth consecutive year in the Commission for Corporate Partnership’s Win-Win Growth Index evaluation. Yoon Hong Huh, CEO of GS E&C, delivers opening remarks at the "Grand Partners Fiesta 2026," held on the 12th of last month. GS E&C previously also received the highest rating for the fourth consecutive year in the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s evaluation of mutual cooperation among construction companies. The Win-Win Growth Index combines the Commission for Corporate Partnership’s comprehensive evaluation of shared growth with the Fair Trade Commission’s evaluation of compliance with fair trade agreements. It rates and publicly classifies large companies’ shared-growth performance into five categories: highest, excellent, average, below average, and very poor. Companies receiving the highest rating are eligible for benefits including a two-year exemption from the Fair Trade Commission’s ex officio investigations in the subcontracting sector, extra points in the Public Procurement Service’s preliminary qualification review (PQ) for public tenders, and preferential treatment when the National Tax Service selects exemplary taxpayers. GS E&C operates its own shared-growth cooperation programs to establish fair business practices with partner companies and promote sustainable growth. It provides various forms of support that partner companies can see and feel in practice, focusing on four areas: ▲compliance management and the establishment of fair trade practices ▲financial and management support ▲strengthening partner companies’ competitiveness ▲promoting horizontal communication. With safety as its top priority, GS E&C pays industrial safety and health management costs in advance and helps cover the cost of assigning dedicated safety personnel to high-risk construction work. It has also worked to strengthen its partners’ safety and quality capabilities and competitiveness, including by introducing a fair competitive bidding system in 2021 to help them secure reasonable profits and maintain stable operations. GS E&C also continues to provide financial support to help partner companies stabilize their operations and strengthen their competitiveness. Each year, it provides KRW 15 billion in interest-free management support and operates a KRW 30 billion shared-growth fund. It also provides support through an annual KRW 4 billion shared-growth cooperation fund for small and medium-sized partners’ technology and research and development, productivity improvements, workforce development, and training. A GS E&C representative said, "Receiving the highest rating in the Win-Win Growth Index for the sixth consecutive year reflects external recognition of our sustained efforts to grow together with our partner companies. NINGBO, ZHEJIANG, CHINA, November 10, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — When European procurement managers evaluate cleaning appliances for retail shelves, expectations have shifted away from superficial aesthetic appeal toward rigorous safety verification. In home cleaning and textile maintenance sectors, electrical safety, temperature rise control, and mechanical protection have become strict baseline metrics. Buyers no longer select products based solely on suction power numbers; instead, they examine how internal components withstand continuous operational stress. Within this shifting trade environment, Yiwu Saiwei Household Appliances Co., Ltd. (Amare) has established a robust operational foothold by aligning manufacturing precision with international safety expectations. As a specialized enterprise focusing on textile maintenance devices, Amare operates as a China leading carpet spot cleaning machine supplier, addressing the rigorous demands of global distribution networks through systematic quality control. The contemporary supply chain environment places considerable emphasis on verifiable reliability at the factory level. Retailers across Western Europe and North America scrutinize supplier credentials down to individual component tolerances and circuit board layouts. When sourcing a carpet spot cleaning machine, procurement teams look for manufacturers who can demonstrate consistent output without compromising on electrical insulation or thermal management. This operational reality requires production facilities to maintain tight tolerances during plastic injection molding, motor assembly, and wiring harness installation. By integrating advanced testing instruments directly into production lines, manufacturing plants can filter out potential defects before final packaging. The Significance of GS Certification in European Markets Quality assurance frameworks in export destinations rely heavily on recognized third-party safety marks. The GS mark, standing for Geprüfte Sicherheit, represents an authoritative German safety certification recognized throughout the European Union. Tested strictly against European Norm standards by accredited independent testing institutions, this mark verifies that a product meets statutory safety requirements regarding mechanical strength, electrical insulation, ergonomic design, and chemical composition. Although the GS mark is technically voluntary under European product legislation, major German retailers, DIY warehouse chains, and regional distributors treat it as a mandatory prerequisite for market entry. Compared to the CE marking, which relies primarily on manufacturer self-declaration, the GS mark requires factory inspections and independent laboratory testing of physical samples. This distinction makes GS certification a formidable benchmark for overseas suppliers seeking entry into premium retail channels. Retail buyers recognize that products bearing this safety mark have undergone rigorous evaluation regarding potential hazards such as short circuits, overheating, user burns, and toxic material emissions. Consequently, achieving GS compliance transforms a standard household appliance into a trusted consumer commodity. Manufacturers who invest in this certification demonstrate a long-term commitment to consumer protection and regulatory transparency, distinguishing their offerings in crowded retail environments. How Precision Manufacturing Supports GS Compliance Meeting stringent German safety standards requires meticulous attention to engineering and internal component design. At its manufacturing facility in Zhejiang, Yiwu Saiwei Household Appliances Co., Ltd. implements dedicated engineering protocols to ensure that every device meets mechanical and electrical safety requirements. The company’s core product lineup includes versatile 500W spot cleaning units engineered for deep textile extraction. These compact machines utilize proprietary self-developed water pumps and heating elements designed to balance cleaning efficiency with thermal stability during extended operation cycles. To prevent fluid ingress into sensitive electrical compartments, these 500W units feature a deliberate clean and wastewater separation architecture. The dual-tank configuration isolates fresh cleaning solution from extracted wastewater, preventing cross-contamination and reducing the risk of internal short circuits. Furthermore, integrated overflow prevention sensors automatically halt water intake when recovery tanks reach maximum capacity. Motor overheating protection mechanisms monitor operational temperatures in real time, cutting power supply automatically if thermal thresholds are exceeded due to restricted airflow or extended continuous use. Beyond internal fluid dynamics, the structural integrity of the appliance plays a critical role in mechanical safety. Precision metal and plastic molds ensure that housing components maintain exact wall thicknesses and tight assembly clearances. This dimensional consistency eliminates loose panel gaps where moisture or dust could penetrate internal circuitry. Strain reliefs on power cords and secure internal wiring harnesses prevent wire fraying or disconnection under mechanical vibration. By combining robust thermal management, precise fluid isolation, and durable mechanical housing, Amare ensures that its carpet spot cleaning machine achieves the structural reliability necessary to pass rigorous GS laboratory evaluations. A credible safety certification is only as reliable as the manufacturing consistency behind it. To maintain continuous compliance with European standards, export suppliers must implement comprehensive batch tracking and quality traceability systems. In modern factory operations, accountability extends from raw material intake to final packaging and palletization. Each manufactured unit receives a unique laser-etched serial number and production batch barcode, linking the finished appliance to specific material lots, component suppliers, and assembly shift logs. When independent auditors inspect production facilities for GS surveillance audits, they examine these traceability records to verify that mass-produced items match the exact specifications of the original tested prototype. Critical components such as thermostats, power switches, pump motors, and internal wiring cables are sourced from qualified tier-one suppliers with verifiable material test reports. Yiwu Saiwei Household Appliances Co., Ltd. archives all incoming material inspection certificates and end-of-line electrical safety test logs in a centralized digital database. This rigorous documentation process enables channel distributors and retail buyers to trace safety data instantly if quality inquiries arise. If a specific batch requires verification, quality assurance personnel can retrieve electrical insulation test results, high-voltage breakdown test records, and functional test logs within minutes. This level of operational transparency reassures commercial partners that product safety is managed through systematic engineering protocols rather than random spot checks. Such structured traceability reinforces long-term trust between Chinese manufacturing enterprises and international trade partners. The evolution of household appliance procurement demonstrates that sustainable export success relies on uncompromising safety compliance and precise manufacturing control. As international buyers raise expectations regarding electrical safety and mechanical durability, suppliers must anchor their operations in verifiable engineering standards. Amare has positioned itself at the forefront of this movement by embedding strict quality protocols into every stage of production, from raw material inspection to finished product testing. By mastering the technical requirements of GS certification, the company delivers reliable cleaning solutions that meet the exacting standards of European retailers and commercial distributors. Business partners seeking a dependable carpet spot cleaning machine supplier will find that meticulous engineering and transparent quality control create a solid foundation for long-term collaboration. title: Learnings from Earnings - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content:
Third-quarter earnings have so far demonstrated resilience. However, as investors begin to look toward 2027, the reporting season is increasingly distinguishing companies with durable demand, visible returns on investment, and pricing power from those where growth comes at an increasingly high cost. Earnings growth is broadening beyond the small group of companies that have dominated market returns in recent years. Beneath headline figures, this is a much more differentiated season. In our view, strong demand across AI infrastructure and industrial suppliers has not always translated into strong earnings, while impressive beats sometimes proved less impressive on closer inspection. Furthermore, markets are not always rewarding solid fundamentals amid volatility. Positive earnings surprises have received relatively muted reactions, while misses have continued to be punished. We believe it is particularly important to distinguish short-term share-price reactions from the durability of the underlying business. We believe over time, companies that convert demand into sustainable margins and free cash flow, protect pricing power through differentiated offerings, and deliver against credible commitments should be better placed to earn market recognition. Investors increasingly want to understand whether demand can be met and how efficiently it converts into margins, free cash flow and ultimately shareholder returns. AI infrastructure may potentially be the clearest example. Major cloud businesses are collectively running at roughly $440 billion of annualized revenues, with growth exceeding 50% year-on-year, while demand continues to exceed available capacity. Expected capital expenditure among five of the largest AI infrastructure spenders has risen to approximately $1.16 trillion for 2027, compared with roughly $800 billion this year.1 The debate has shifted from the willingness to invest toward the ability to fund, deliver and ultimately monetize that investment. In the financial sector, leadership at one major asset manager noted that they are seeing a genuine shortage of capital for the first time in decades as governments and corporations fund this generational AI buildout, creating potential opportunities to position compute and GPU financing as the next major asset class.2 Across the semiconductor ecosystem, supply remains tight, but scarcity is creating strategic choices, forcing companies to protect long-term customer relationships rather than simply maximizing short-term pricing. Meanwhile, industrial companies are acting as the physical backbone of this buildout. Several building-products and industrial services firms are experiencing exceptionally strong demand, with data-center orders surging.3 Yet, despite massive top-line beats, margin conversion is proving to be the real test. Companies are facing significantly higher input-cost pressures, and gross margins are sometimes missing consensus expectations despite booming revenues. We believe AI is becoming a test not simply of technological leadership, but of capital and operational discipline. Two companies may participate in the same structural growth market but generate dramatically different returns depending on how much they pay for capacity and how efficiently they utilize it. We believe the next generation of AI winners will increasingly be determined by balance-sheet capacity, pricing discipline, and return on invested capital, with companies that successfully convert exceptional order books into clean margin expansions standing to outperform. The consumer story is more nuanced than a simple debate about strength or weakness. Aggregate spending remains healthy, but consumers appear increasingly deliberate about what they buy and what constitutes value. Major payments networks continue to demonstrate healthy aggregates, with one major network reporting US payments volumes up 10% and cross-border spending up 14%, and another reporting global payment volumes up 7%.4 Underneath these healthy aggregates, behavior is changing. Financial institutions note that retail accounts are growing, but trading activity per account has seen a broad-based slowdown. Restaurant businesses are seeing diners protect the core meal while cutting back on alcohol or dessert, and buy-now-pay-later volumes have surged 25%, giving consumers another way to manage cash flow without abandoning purchases.5 There is also evidence of strength at both ends of the spectrum, with value laundry products gaining share for one consumer-goods company, while another is seeing growth in premium toothpaste. The same dynamic is playing out in other sectors. Industrial and materials companies are reporting instances where input cost inflation is slightly exceeding pricing power, potentially creating margin headwinds. With consumers and end-buyers more price-sensitive, we believe companies are increasingly focused on protecting value, meaning the answer is no longer to simply pass input costs through to the customer. We favor companies with multiple levers to solve the value equation and strong internal productivity to absorb input cost pressures, rather than relying on broad-based pricing that could alienate a discerning end-user. At a time when investors are scrutinizing the durability of earnings into 2027 and beyond, contracted demand, backlogs and capacity commitments are becoming potentially more increasingly valuable. One leading memory manufacturer has long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of planned 2027-2028 capacity, creating an unusual degree of visibility for an industry historically characterized by pronounced cycles. Further downstream, cloud providers are reporting order backlogs north of $578 billion, with visibility extending into 2028 and parts of 2029. 6 The phenomenon extends deeply into European and US industrials. One building products company now boasts a $23 billion backlog, giving management greater confidence in delivering double-digit organic growth next year because so much demand is already secured. A European machinery company saw mining equipment orders surge 31%, while a global distributor reported that its US data-center backlog now exceeds $3 billion.7 Not all visibility is equal, however, as contracted revenues differ from capacity reservations, which differ again from order backlogs or management guidance. In our view, strong visibility only creates value if companies can fulfill that demand at attractive margins. For investors the distinction between growth that is forecast and growth that is increasingly underwritten is important. In an uncertain environment, credible visibility into future revenues and cash flows commands an increasing premium. We prefer companies with underwritten growth, expanding structural backlogs, and proven execution capabilities. In technology, we will continue looking beyond AI infrastructure spending toward adoption, monetization and returns, asking whether strong demand can translate into sustainable revenues, margins and free cash flow. In consumer sectors, holiday-sensitive companies may provide further evidence on traffic, promotional intensity and pricing, and whether increasingly selective consumers are responding to affordability initiatives. Recent results suggest that supporting volumes through price investment can come at a meaningful cost to margins. Meanwhile, utilities and energy should provide further insight into the second-order effects of the AI investment cycle, including power demand, funding requirements and capital discipline, while energy companies face continued scrutiny over the balance between reinvestment, balance-sheet repair and shareholder distributions. Overall, we are watching for evidence of durable demand, pricing power, capital discipline, and credible 2027 guidance. With positive surprises receiving relatively muted rewards while misses continue to be punished, the remainder of the season may reinforce the importance of distinguishing between companies delivering growth and those converting it into sustainable returns. 1 Company reports. title: Last Orders in the Alps: Riding a BMW R 1300 GS through the Dolomites - Autocar India
content: Somewhere on the approach to Passo Falzarego, I kept the throttle open well beyond the sensible braking point, then feathered the brakes far too late and tipped the fully loaded 250kg BMW R 1300 GS into a corner. The horizon tilted at what felt like 49 degrees. The motorcycle took it all in its stride. The suspension swallowed the bend; when I rolled back onto the throttle, the Akrapovič exhaust cleared its throat, the traction control moderated the conversation between the drive shaft and the rear wheel, and the front wheel lifted in a little wheelie of triumph. I carried on to the next hairpin with a smile plastered across my face, as it had been so many times that week. Around me, the Dolomites were having the best week of their year, in the middle of October. The larches had turned gold and rust, the pale rock towers stood bathed in sunshine, and the tarmac was dry and, for long stretches, entirely ours. Every so often another rider came the other way, two fingers held out in the wordless handshake motorcyclists everywhere seem to have agreed on. And there, around the next hairpin, a thought arrived, uninvited and slightly absurd: all of this had begun with an innocent phone call from Abhijit, my brother-in-law. Abhijit was twiddling thumbs between jobs, with time on his hands and a recently purchased Ducati Multistrada V4S standing in his parking bay. He called me for advice on where to take it for a road trip. The conversation wandered from Goa to Rajasthan, and to Kerala, but none of that caught his fancy. Then he said, “What about riding to Ladakh?” I told him that riding in Ladakh is wonderful, but getting there from Mumbai is tiresome. “It’s not like Europe,” I said rather offhandedly, “where riding from Munich to the Alps is almost as enjoyable as riding in them.” That was the tipping point. The Alps stuck to the conversation like a rash, and the mere mention of them infused my voice with a whole new level of excitement and elation. By the end of the call, what had started as Abhijit’s search for a week-long ride had turned into a plot in which I had committed to planning a 12-day loop out of Munich through Germany, Switzerland, Italy and Austria, with me becoming a party to the plan. Those eight minutes on the phone ultimately ended up costing me Rs 2.5 lakh – money very well spent! Then I started looking for a motorcycle. My first instinct was to find something in the 600cc to 800cc category. But my former Autocar India colleague, Ouseph Chacko, now a BMW-certified GS instructor, and Rishaad Mody, this magazine’s motorcycle editor, were unanimous in their advice: “Take the BMW R 1300 GS. It’s a sweet, sweet motorcycle.” That was all the convincing I needed. I asked BMW for one, and they said yes. Abhijit also chose the GS and rented one for the trip. To plan our ride, I hopped, skipped and jumped between Google Maps, Auntie Claude and Booking.com, checking distances, looking for route advice and good food, and finding mostly affordable two-bedroom apartments with free cancellation as close to the day of stay as possible. Now, on a bend near Passo Falzarego, with the larches blazing, the great limestone walls of the Dolomites bathed in warm, slanting sunlight, and the road empty beneath a motorcycle that was mine for twelve days, I smiled wistfully at the phone call that had started it all. Nine days earlier, I had stepped off an Etihad flight in Munich after an intentional 24-hour break in Abu Dhabi, so I met the GS without a trace of jet lag. The comfortable cabin, attentive service and warm hospitality onboard meant I swung a leg over the saddle well rested and energetic. We left Munich and rode south, deeper into Bavaria, the Alps growing larger in my visor until Wallgau, a village of timbered balconies and painted house fronts, appeared at their foot. For dinner that evening at the Gasthof Zur Post, I did what any traveller in Bavaria is duty-bound to do and ordered the pork knuckle. It arrived beneath a cap of crackling the size of a small cushion and left as bare bones. The next day, Austria’s Fernpass and Reschenpass unspooled in long, flowing curves, easy miles in which to settle into the GS before the real work began. Then we dropped into the Italian part of Tyrol and spent two nights in Laces, in the Vinschgau Valley, among apple orchards so laden that the branches were propped up on crutches. This also meant delicious apple strudel at most places we ate at. Carrying on, we crossed into Switzerland, over the Ofenpass and through the Swiss National Park, on a road lined with pine forest and almost no traffic, before dropping down to Poschiavo, with the Bernina Pass on its doorstep. I had set the mode button to toggle between Dynamic for the long, easy stretches, Dynamic Pro for the passes, and Rain for wet-weather days. By then, my thumb knew which one to reach for before my head did. Crossing back into Italy, we spent a night near Bormio, and the next morning we came face to face with the mighty Passo Stelvio sitting at 2,757 metres (9,045 feet). We rode the famed 48 hairpins of the north face. At the Tibet Hütte, the café at the summit, I ate apple strudel with fresh cream and watched cyclists grind up the last bends under their own power, grunting at the effort. I prayed to the Almighty to cure them of this affliction that makes them torture themselves and took another bite of my delicious dessert. At the bottom of the Stelvio, we turned east through the Vinschgau, past Merano and Bolzano, and powered on to Villandro and the Dolomites. Rumpelehof stands in the hamlet of Stofls, on the outskirts of Villandro. It is a working farm with self-catering apartments, where Alexandra and Raimund Gasser raise cattle and sheep. Mornings began with bleats and bull bellows rather than an alarm. Our two-bedroom apartment looked straight across at the Dolomites, a spectacular view, especially at sunrise. There were apple trees on the farm, and Raimund told me I could eat the apples without washing them because no pesticide had been sprayed on them. The only thing to watch for was worms. They were delicious, the apples, not the worms. For dinner on both evenings, we rode down to Gasthof Pizzeria Rustica in Villandro, a sprawling, warmly lit place that unfolds room after room, each one fuller and louder than the last. We came across two lads from Punjab working in its kitchen and had a hearty conversation with them. It was hunting season, so game crowded the menu. One night I ate a pizza with local salami and fiery peppers, the heat sneaking up like a rumour. The next, I had tagliatelle with a deer ragù – rich, slow-cooked, laced with pepper and finished with Parmigiano Reggiano – that I would happily have crossed a mountain pass for. Fortunately, I only had to ride down a hill. On our first day there, we rode a loop from the farm through Ponte Gardena, Ortisei and Selva, then up Passo Sella to Canazei, over the Pordoi and back the same way. The Alps had been wonderful, but it was the Dolomites that took my heart, perhaps because we arrived just as the autumn colours peaked. Near Canazei, through my helmet, I heard a familiar thump. My heart told me what it was before I turned my head. Sure enough, a Royal Enfield was chugging up towards Passo Pordoi. I excitedly flagged it down. The rider, from Lake Garda, said he loved everything about India and Royal Enfield. Around us were Multistradas, GSs and Africa Twins, while this humble Bullet chugged up the slope, holding its own, its rider in no hurry at all. The two engines could hardly have been more different. His Bullet, a single cylinder that thumps. Mine, a boxer, with two cylinders poking out either side like elbows at a crowded table, a layout BMW has been refining since 1923. Blip the throttle at a standstill and the GS rocks sideways, like a large dog shifting its weight. Both are unmistakable, and both certainly have character. It was the kind of day that leaves you a little melancholic and nostalgic, quietly happy at the way things have turned out. So, the next morning, when I leaned the GS into the hairpin on the road to Falzarego that opened this story, my mind went back to Abhijit’s phone call and how a casual conversation about Ladakh had brought me here. Mornings at that altitude start with a nip in the air, which is where the GS earns some of its keep. Thumb the heated grips and seat into life, and within two minutes you are sitting on a warm bench with warm hands, wondering why anyone ever thought bravery had anything to do with riding Alpine passes in mid-October. The other quiet hero was the BMW Motorrad ConnectedRide Navigator, the GPS unit above the dash, which I came to treat as a third member of the expedition. It is controlled by the rotary dial just ahead of the left grip, so I never had to take a glove off or a hand off the bars. I had loaded the daily routes I’d planned at home. Twelve GPX files, one for each day, went in through the BMW Motorrad Connected app, and every morning, the unit simply knew where we were going. Better still, it let me tell the motorcycle what kind of road I wanted: very twisty, moderately twisty or sensibly straight. I could ask it to avoid motorways and toll roads altogether. Where an ordinary satnav would have hustled us down the fastest road, this one, with a little encouragement from my thumb, kept finding the road worth riding. Over twelve days, it took us on a string of roads I would never have found on my own. That was how we found the road to Passo Falzarego and a procession of bends I’d happily call unreasonable, in the best way. Auntie Claude had warned me of the possibility of closed passes and snow. The passes, evidently, had not got her memo. Falzarego led to Passo Giau, which, as many riders will agree, is the most beautiful pass in the Dolomites. The road climbs through hairpin after hairpin into a wide, bare bowl ringed by rock, and the GS went up it as if it had been waiting all week for the invitation. Part of the secret is the boxer’s low, wide cylinders, which pull the centre of gravity down, so a motorcycle this heavy turns in like something much lighter. I braked late, leaned into corners at angles that would make Newton neurotic and got back on the throttle early, delighted by the feel of the front wheel lifting. We stopped at the top for coffee and cake, the two BMWs parked in the sun and preening. From there, we descended through Val di Zoldo, stopping at Rifugio San Sebastiano for a hearty salami and cheese sandwich and indulgent hot chocolate on Passo Duran, then continued to Venas di Cadore. We were meant to stay the night in the town of San Vito di Cadore, but our booking was cancelled because my credit card payment hadn’t gone through. It turned out to be the best thing my card did all year. A last-minute scramble found us a room at Dolomiti Lodge Villa Gaia, in a village ten kilometres away, and it became the best stay of the trip. We walked in expecting a bed and a plate of pasta. We walked out feeling like regulars at a village wedding. Dinner that evening at the lodge’s restaurant felt like one long communal table. Everyone talked to everyone, even to us, though we knew no Italian, rounds of drinks were bought for us, and people drifted over to say hello. Most of the diners were locals who knew the staff, but nobody treated us as outsiders. The staff came from Albania, Italy, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and they worked the room like a well-rehearsed dance. Music played, feet skipped between tables, and now and then a waitress broke into a small pirouette on her way to the kitchen. It was joyful, noisy and entirely unpretentious. The food kept pace. I opted for the wild pigeon, a bird I was trying for the first time. Where I come from, pigeons are treated as a civic nuisance, so there was a certain poetic justice in the exercise. It was really very good. Villa Gaia was the southernmost point and the happiest evening of our trip, and without anyone saying so, it became the hinge. From there, every road pointed north and back towards Munich. We still rode some glorious ones: from Cortina into East Tyrol, a night at Bergmanns Ferienapartment in Debant, a day on the Grossglockner High Alpine Road in Austria, then Kitzbühel and St. Johann in Tirol. The colours stayed blazing, the roads stayed dry, and the GS kept doling out delight. But the mood of the trip had undergone a subtle change. The days that had begun with a hunger to reach the next pass now began with the gentle awareness that this was the home run, and that real life, with its emails and credit card bills, was waiting somewhere beyond the Bavarian border. It is an odd feeling, fully enjoying something and mourning it at the same time. And then we rolled back into Munich, and I hauled the BMW R 1300 GS onto the main stand for the final time. Twelve days earlier, I had been apprehensive about handling this big motorcycle. Now I unloaded my luggage with the sort of reluctance people usually reserve for goodbyes at airports. I gave the tank one last pat, fondly, and walked away. The Key Monastery blends into Spiti’s spectacular landscape. title: GS Law mobilizes 2nd regional leg of West PH Sea Maritime Security Forum in Tarlac - University of Santo Tomas
content: The UST Graduate School of Law, in collaboration with the Tarlac State University School of Law, concluded the 2nd Regional leg of the West Philippine Sea Arbitral Ruling Forum on November 6, 2026, at the Old SP Session Hall, Capitol Building in Tarlac. The title of the second forum was “Upholding Sovereignty Through Law: Diplomacy, United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and the Rationale of the 2016 Arbitral Award.” Former Supreme Court Associate Justice Hon. Francis H. Jardeleza and Atty. Jewel Dela Cruz shared their expertise as speakers, with Atty. Carisa Balilia providing thoughtful insights as a reactor. The lecture gave enriching perspectives on the legal, diplomatic, and historical foundations of the Philippines’ maritime rights in the contested sea. The initiative aimed to mobilize Filipino voices and entrusted the potential second case against China to the youth. Jardeleza served as the Solicitor General (2012–2014) and led the Philippine legal team in the landmark UNCLOS maritime arbitration against China. The first Regional Leg of the forum, titled “Batangas Securing the Maritime Frontier: Strategic Defense,” was held last Oct. 23, 2026, in collaboration with the University of Batangas College of Law. Anchored on the overall theme “Upholding Sovereignty Through Law: Diplomacy, UNCLOS, and the Rationale of the 2016 Arbitral Award,” the program brought together an engaged audience of law students, fisherfolk, TSU officials, the Armed Forces of the Philippines, legal practitioners, and advocates for an insightful and meaningful discussion. The third and last leg, titled “People at the Frontline: Building Resilient Coastal Communities amid West Philippine Sea Tensions”, will be staged at the Palawan State University on January 29, 2027. With support from the Public Diplomacy Section of the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the caravan kicked off at the UST on Sept. 25. 2026. It was spearheaded by GS Law and the Faculty of Civil Law, together with the UST Research and Endowment Foundation, Inc. The University of Santo Tomas is one of the leading private research universities in the Philippines and is consistently ranked among the top 1000 universities in the whole world. With academic degrees and research thrusts in the natural, health, applied, social, and sacred sciences, as well as business and management, the University continuously strives to make a positive impact on the society.
